analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying Congress for life.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the federal criminal code to replace the current 'cooling-off' rules — former Senators face a two-year lobbying ban and former House members a one-year ban — with a permanent, lifetime ban on former Members of Congress making lobbying contacts with anyone in either chamber of Congress. Violations would be subject to fines or imprisonment. It also added a one-year ban for former elected officers of the House. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer see former lawmakers cash in on their relationships with the colleagues they just served alongside. lobbyists who hire ex-Members for their access would lose their most valuable recruits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters tired of the lobbying revolving door

how_it_helps.text: It would make it a federal crime, punishable by fines or imprisonment, for any former Senator or Representative to make a lobbying contact with any Member, officer, or employee of either chamber of Congress, at any time after leaving office.
It would replace today's short bans — two years for former Senators, one year for former House members — with a permanent ban, and add a one-year ban for former elected House officers.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would lose a lucrative post-Congress career path built on their inside access.

drawbacks.text: The ban is broad and permanent for former Members, raising the concern that it could deter former lawmakers from ordinary advocacy work or go further than the narrow 'cooling-off' rationale requires.
Even before it was introduced, critics could argue a lifetime lobbying ban might push former Members to influence their former colleagues indirectly rather than eliminate the influence trade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, documented conflict of interest — former lawmakers selling access to their old colleagues — and its cost was limited to former members' earning options. Its main design weakness is that it was narrow: it covered congressional contacts but left the larger revolving door into the executive branch and the broader lobbying industry untouched, so influence could still flow through allies and former staff.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled it for consideration before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 12, 2015 by Rep. Cicilline and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On March 16, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and former Members of Congress, who kept a two-year or one-year 'cooling-off' rule instead of a lifetime ban and retained a lucrative career path after leaving office.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban former Members of Congress from lobbying Congress for life.

for.name: Rep. Dave Loebsack
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 16, 2015 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Former lawmakers are among the most valuable hires at lobbying firms because of their personal relationships on Capitol Hill. A permanent ban would cut off that recruiting pipeline, which is why the industry benefits from the bill staying buried.

industries.industry: Former Members of Congress (as a class)
industries.note: The bill would bar former lawmakers from ever selling their access to current congressional staff and members, eliminating a lucrative post-Congress career path that ordinary citizens have no equivalent of.
